faq.a: Approaches such as synthetic or external control arms built from real world data exist, but regulators accept them only in limited circumstances and with strong justification.
faq.q: Can AI replace a control group?

faq.a: Not separately. But if AI produces data the FDA will rely on, the sponsor must be able to show the model is credible for that use, and should discuss it with the agency early.
faq.q: Does using AI in a trial need FDA approval?

name: Clinical Development and Trials
blurb: AI in trial design, recruitment, data management and the AI designed drugs now in trials.
title: Clinical Development and Trials
answer: AI is used to design protocols, find and match patients, clean and analyse trial data and draft study documents. The first AI derived drug candidates are moving through the clinic, but most are still in early phases, and the trial results so far are what will decide whether AI shortens drug development.

reading.body:
AI in clinical trials is delivering operational speed, not yet proven drugs: of 63 companies with AI derived candidates in human trials, 60 finished phase 1 and only 8 finished phase 2.

The pattern is a widening gap between activity and evidence. Recruitment, data cleaning and document drafting save weeks without changing the science, which is why they are the fastest gains. The clinical bet is separate and slower. One AI discovered drug, rentosertib, met its phase 2a goals in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, and one AI engineered antibody, GB-0895, has reached phase 3. Those are single results, and the ASCO count shows how few candidates have survived the middle of the pipeline where most drugs fail.

This matters for AI because the compute behind these programs is only justified if candidates clear later phases. Trial design, patient matching and data management are software workloads that scale with the same data centre capacity as any other enterprise AI. The drug candidates themselves are the test of whether that capacity buys shorter development times, and that question is settled in clinics, not in data centres.

The data does not cover cost, trial duration, or how many of the 63 companies are still active. It does not say whether the 8 phase 2 completions succeeded. It also does not quantify how much time the operational uses actually save, only that they are described as the fastest gains.

explainer:
Clinical trials are where most of a medicine's development time and cost goes. A trial must be designed, approved, staffed at hospital sites, filled with eligible patients, run for months or years, and its data cleaned, analysed and reported. Delays at any step push the whole programme back, and patient recruitment is the most common reason trials run late.

AI is being applied at each stage. In design, models help test whether a protocol is feasible and whether its eligibility criteria will find enough patients. In recruitment, natural language processing matches patient records against complex criteria far faster than manual review. During the trial, AI helps clean data, flag anomalies and monitor sites, and generative models draft study documents. Afterwards, real world data from health records is increasingly used alongside trial data, with AI extracting the clinical details hidden in free text.

The rules depend on what the AI does. Operational uses, such as drafting documents or scheduling, mainly need ordinary quality controls. Uses that generate evidence a regulator will rely on, such as identifying outcomes or supporting dose decisions, fall under the FDA's credibility framework and Good Clinical Practice. Regulators are also changing how they work, with the FDA moving toward seeing trial data in real time.

The other half of this section is the trials of AI derived medicines themselves, which will show whether AI makes drugs more likely to succeed.
key_points: Recruitment is the biggest cause of delay and the clearest win for AI matching.
AI supports protocol design, data cleaning, monitoring and document drafting.
AI that produces regulatory evidence needs credibility evidence under FDA expectations and GCP.
Real world data extracted with AI increasingly supplements trial data.
AI derived drugs are mostly in early phases; late stage results are still to come.
